meta.title: Twelve moves toward a leaner Dossier
meta.lede: Six small and six large, and one decision before any of them: reshape the current code or rebuild the core from its pieces. Each move says how it works, what the reader gets, what the agent does, what it unlocks, and what it costs. The theme is subtraction: fewer controls, fewer blocks, one export, one look. Pick by number.

parts.markdown:
Strip away the 43 blocks, the packs, the workspaces, and the release evidence, and Dossier does three things. An agent turns a prompt into a structured document. A person reads that document and decides inside it. The agent reads the decisions back and acts. Everything else in the codebase exists to serve one of those three, and anything that serves none of them is weight.

The strongest use today is the one you described: ask an agent for a plan with minor and major features, get a page you can skim and pick from, reply with numbers. That loop is Dossier's front door. 0.7 should make that loop excellent first, then let the same skeleton carry plans, reviews, releases, and incidents without changing how the page feels.

Four principles for the release:

1. The static file is for reading and deciding. Authoring, editing, and studio tools live in `dossier serve`.
2. One page shape, many kinds. A brainstorm and an incident review share the same shell, table of contents, facets, and summary table.
3. Every control on the page must be explainable in one sentence to someone who opened the file cold.
4. Budgets are features. The runtime, the stylesheet, and the block catalog each get a number, and the number goes down.

The 0.5 and 0.6 arcs shipped every idea from the June brainstorm. Each one made sense alone. Together they produced a reader shell that carries authoring tools, six overlapping export concepts, and a runtime that every artifact pays for whether it uses it or not. Measured on the showcase example:

spec.label: 7 controls
spec.text: In the top bar: search, Edit, Blocks, Evidence, Theme Studio, theme toggle, Export. Four of them change the document rather than read it.

spec.label: 11 items
spec.text: In the Export menu, plus 14 more buttons inside the Export Center. Source, state, merged, handoff, prompt, digest, and Markdown are seven names for two ideas.

spec.label: 5 modals
spec.text: Export Center, block editor, evidence form, source viewer, shortcuts, and the palette ship in every file, including read-only briefs.

spec.label: 74 KB
spec.text: Runtime JavaScript inlined into every artifact. Most of it handles state packets, imports, and the block editor.

spec.label: 67 KB
spec.text: Inlined CSS: base tokens, the skin layer, theme packs, and per-block styles for all 43 blocks regardless of which appear.

spec.label: 43 blocks
spec.text: Fifteen of them are process variants that overlap: four kinds of board, four kinds of evidence, two kinds of diff, two kinds of gate.

spec.label: 385 KB
spec.text: The showcase file. The typical example lands near 145 KB, of which the document model is under 20 KB.

spec.label: 28 tools
spec.text: On the MCP server, reading and writing ten packet schemas. The June brainstorm asked for four: create, render, read decisions, apply decisions.

spec.label: 2 renderers
spec.text: A 1,600-line string renderer and a 1,350-line React port that must stay in step for every block.

parts.markdown:
Taken together, the twelve moves below are a rebuild. The honest question is whether to do that rebuild inside the current tree, one subtraction at a time, or to stand up a new core beside it from the pieces worth keeping and cut over when the examples build. Both paths end at the same product. They differ in how long the code is in a half state and in what we let ourselves keep by accident.

A clean core would rest on five concepts, and nothing on the page would exist outside them:

1. **Kind.** A preset naming the sections a document has, the facets its items carry, and how the reader replies.
2. **Section.** Prose, a table, code, a diagram, a figure, a chart, a callout, or a board. Content blocks, no state.
3. **Item.** A numbered thing inside a board with a title, a one-line summary, size, effort, impact, dependencies, and facets.
4. **Facet.** A labeled paragraph on an item, in the fixed order the kind defines.
5. **Decision.** What the reader said about an item: picked or not, a verdict, a note. The only state the file ever holds.

Everything the current product does maps onto these. A release checklist is a board whose items are gates and whose decision is done or not. An incident review is a board of findings with a timeline section in front. A patch review is a board of files whose facet is a diff. The concepts do not grow with the use cases; the kinds do, and a kind is forty lines.

spec.label: model
spec.text: One JSON schema for kind, meta, sections, items, facets, and decisions. Stable ids everywhere. Old block type names accepted as aliases so every existing file still builds.

spec.label: kinds
spec.text: Six presets shipped, custom kinds loadable from a pack. Each one is a small readable file, not code.

spec.label: renderer
spec.text: One string renderer, zero runtime dependencies. The React package becomes a typed wrapper that embeds the rendered document, so there is one renderer to keep correct.

spec.label: reader
spec.text: The runtime that ships in the file: table of contents, search, palette, theme, collapse, copy, decisions, pick. Under 20 KB, assembled from the modules the page needs.

spec.label: studio
spec.text: Everything that edits: in-place text, block order, evidence, accent preview, patch import, CodeMirror. Injected by serve, never in the file.

spec.label: agent
spec.text: The skill plus four MCP tools: create from a kind, render, read decisions, apply decisions. Workspaces, release evidence, and packs keep their commands and consume the same two output files.

spec.label: build-time
spec.text: Kept as is: Shiki, Graphviz, KaTeX, the unified diff parser, DOCX and PDF export, the CLI, the test suite, and the examples as parity fixtures.

parts.markdown: The rebuild path in practice: create the new core beside the old one, port content blocks first against the examples, then boards and decisions, then the reader runtime, then serve. Cut over when every example builds and renders through the new core, delete the old tree, and ship that as 0.7. The old tree stays readable in git as reference the whole time. Expect three to four weeks against roughly the same for the twelve moves done in place, with less time spent half-broken.

Two documents describe the target. The June brainstorm gave each idea a how-it-works, an experience, a why, and an unlocks line inside a review board. The front door page gave each feature fixed facets, a size chip, an effort chip, an impact meter, a summary table, and a closing call to pick by number. Merged, they become the `brainstorm` kind, and the facet vocabulary generalizes to every kind.

rows: **Reader**, what the person deciding sees and does
**Agent**, what the model does to author or act on it
Size chip, effort chip, impact meter
**Pick** block: numbers plus notes, copied as text and JSON
parts.note: This page is the merged format, now rendered by Dossier from JSON.

parts.markdown: The front door layout becomes Dossier's shell. The table of contents moves to the left and goes sticky, the content column keeps a 68ch measure, features are separated by hairlines rather than boxed, and only four things on a page are objects: the facts tile, the layout list, the summary table, and the also-considered rows. The saturated block is the closing pick action.

spec.label: ≥ 1100px
spec.text: Two columns: 224px sticky table of contents, content column, 56px gap, 1180px frame. No right rail, no progress bar, no back-to-top button.

spec.label: 820 to 1099px
spec.text: One column. The table of contents becomes a wrapping row of chip links under the masthead. Masthead keeps two columns.

spec.label: 720 to 819px
spec.text: Masthead stacks. Facets keep the 148px label column.

spec.label: ≤ 719px
spec.text: Facet labels stack above their text. The summary table scrolls inside its own wrapper. Nothing else scrolls sideways.

spec.label: print
spec.text: Table of contents hidden, hairlines kept, page breaks before each feature article.

items.title: Shell reset
items.summary: The static artifact's top bar drops to four things: where you are, search, theme, and one export.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown:
The generated shell keeps crumbs, the search field, the theme toggle, and a single Export menu with three entries: Copy for agent, Download JSON, Print. Edit, Blocks, Evidence, Theme Studio, the dirty-state pill, the reading progress bar, the back-to-top button, and the Export Center all leave the static build. They are reachable only when the file is served from `dossier serve`, which injects them the way it already injects CodeMirror.

The command palette stays, but its command list is built from what is actually on the page, so a brief without decisions never offers "export decisions."

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Opens the file and sees a document, not a workbench. Every visible control does something a reader would want. The keyboard shortcuts list shrinks to five entries that all work.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Nothing changes in authoring. The skill stops describing the Export Center and describes one action: copy for agent.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Item 8 becomes a refactor of code that is already out of the artifact, rather than a rewrite done under the reader's feet.

facets.label: Risk
facets.markdown: People who attach evidence or edit text inside a shared file lose that until they open it in serve. The README should say so in the first paragraph of Live Editing.

items.title: Left table of contents
items.summary: The right rail becomes a sticky left column with grouped, numbered entries, and collapses to a chip row on narrow screens.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown: The existing table-of-contents builder already knows heading levels. It gains groups: kinds declare which sections are frame, which are pickable items, and which are the rest. Pickable items show their number in mono; frame entries show an en dash. Below 1100px the list turns into wrapping chip links and the group labels hide.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Sees the shape of the document before reading it: how many items, which are minor, which are major. Jumps by number. Scroll-spy still highlights the active entry.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Numbers come from item order in the board, so the agent never assigns them by hand.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: The layout in the section above. Also frees the right side of the page, which is why the measure can widen to 68ch without the content column feeling cramped.

items.title: Type and token swap
items.summary: The front door tokens become Dossier's tokens, with the accent moved to Dossier crimson and a light and a dark palette tuned separately.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown:
The token file is rewritten to the thirteen names on this page: bg, paper, ink, muted, line, line-soft, accent, accent-ink, teal, violet, coral, plus the three font stacks. Three-state theming stays exactly as it is here. Body type is Figtree, one italic serif word in the title uses Instrument Serif, and identifiers use JetBrains Mono, each with a real fallback stack.

Web fonts are opt-in with `meta.fonts: "google"` so the default artifact keeps its no-external-assets promise. Without the flag the same scale and spacing render in the system stack, which carries most of the look.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: The page reads as this one does. Light mode is the base, dark mode is retuned rather than inverted, and the toggle wins over the system setting in both directions.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Sets the accent with one field, `meta.theme.accent`, and nothing else. The fifty-token override surface goes away.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Item 11. Once the tokens are this small, skins and theme packs have nothing left to override.

facets.label: Risk
facets.markdown: Crimson as the accent sits close to a coral risk label, so the risk color moves to Dossier's ochre, which is what this page does. Confirm you like the crimson accent here before it becomes the default; blue as on the front door page is the alternative.

items.title: Facets block
items.summary: A definition-list block with a fixed label order, plus size, effort, and impact fields that render as chips and meters.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown: A new `facets` block takes an ordered list of label and body pairs. Board items gain optional `size`, `effort`, and `impact` fields and an optional `facets` array. The renderer draws the meta row, the numbered title, the one-line summary, and the facet list exactly as the articles on this page. A facet labeled Risk or Note takes the colored label.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Every item on every page has the same facets in the same order, so items can be compared by scanning down one label column.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: The skill gives the agent the facet vocabulary per kind and the rule that order never changes. Less prose freedom, more useful output.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Items 5 and 7. The summary table and the kinds are both derived from these fields.

items.title: Summary table from the board
items.summary: The board emits its own summary table above the items: number, title, size, effort, impact, depends on.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown: A board with `summary: true` renders a table before its items, with the legend line generated from whichever fields are present. Titles link to the item anchors. Depends-on values are item numbers and are validated against the board, so a dangling reference fails the build.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Skims one table, decides what to read in full, and jumps. This is the single biggest reading improvement for long plans.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Never writes the table. It comes from the items, so it cannot drift from them.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Item 6, and a facts tile in the masthead that counts minor, major, and also-considered items automatically.

items.title: Pick by number
items.summary: The closing action copies your selection as one line of text an agent can act on, with JSON behind it.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown: A `pick` block closes any board-carrying kind. It renders as the saturated block at the end of this page. Ticking items and leaving notes anywhere above fills it in. Its button copies text like `Picked 1, 3, 4, 7. Notes: 3 keep blue accent.` and the same content as a small JSON object. This replaces the decisions export, the handoff packet, and the prompt export for the reading case.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Reads, ticks, copies one line, pastes it into the thread. No menu, no packet name to learn.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Parses numbers and notes from the line or reads the JSON from the MCP tool. Both say the same thing.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Item 10. Once the reader's output is one line, the export contract can be one shape.

items.title: Kinds as presets
items.summary: A kind fixes the section order, the facet vocabulary, the summary table, and the closing action, so "make me a brainstorm" produces this page.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown:
Six kinds ship in 0.7: `brainstorm`, `plan`, `review`, `release`, `incident`, and `brief`. Each is a small preset file: the frame sections it expects, the facet labels for its items, whether items are numbered, which fields feed the summary table, and what the pick block says. The generator validates a document against its kind and fills defaults, so a brainstorm with no pick block still gets one.

The existing process kinds map onto these: implementation and debug become `plan` with a different facet set; integration-loop becomes `review`.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Opens any Dossier and already knows where the summary is, where the items are, and how to reply. A release checklist and a feature brainstorm feel like the same product.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: The prompt becomes the product. "Create a brainstorm dossier for X with six minor and four major features" is enough because the kind supplies everything else. The skill teaches six sentences, not forty-three blocks.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Item 12. It also makes the block catalog cut in item 9 safe, since kinds tell you which blocks matter.

facets.label: Risk
facets.markdown: Kinds can become a second, hidden block catalog. Keep each preset under 40 lines and readable by a person.

items.title: Two-tier runtime
items.summary: The static file carries a reader runtime under 20 KB; everything that edits the document moves to the served studio.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown:
The runtime splits into a core and per-block modules. Core: table of contents and scroll-spy, search, palette, theme toggle, collapse, per-block copy, and the pick block. Block modules: checkboxes for action items, verdict and notes controls for boards, gate toggles for release checklists. The generator includes a module only when its block appears. Everything else, meaning in-place text editing, the block editor, evidence forms, state import, revision compare, Theme Studio, and CodeMirror, becomes the studio bundle that `dossier serve` injects.

Budgets are enforced by a test: core plus all block modules stays under 20 KB, base CSS under 30 KB, and the test fails when a change crosses the line.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Files open instantly and behave the same everywhere. A brief has no state machinery at all.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Unchanged for authoring. For editing round-trips it targets serve, where the full toolset lives.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: A React port that only has to match the reader runtime. A plugin rule that plugins ship CSS and markup but no runtime, which keeps packs from re-bloating the file.

facets.label: Risk
facets.markdown: The largest change in the release and the one most likely to regress the existing examples. Do it after item 1 has already hidden the surfaces, so the split is mechanical.

items.title: Block consolidation
items.summary: Forty-three blocks become about twenty-two by folding the overlapping process families into one block each, with the old names kept as aliases.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown:
Five families collapse. `board` absorbs review-board, process-board, finding-list, and cycle-board; the item schema carries verdict options and the facets from item 4. `evidence` absorbs evidence-log, verification-run, trust-report, and process-receipt, with an item kind of run, claim, observation, or receipt. `diff` absorbs patch-set and diff-view. `gates` absorbs release-checklist and verdict-gate. `log` absorbs decision-log, comment-thread, upstream-response, and integration-report.

Validation maps the old type names to the new ones with a deprecation warning and rewrites the model, so every existing example builds unchanged. 0.8 removes the aliases.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Fewer visual idioms to learn. A board looks like a board whether it holds features, findings, or work items.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Chooses from a catalog it can hold in context. The cheat sheet fits on one screen.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Roughly a third of the CSS and of the render code goes away. The React port gets smaller by the same amount.

facets.label: Risk
facets.markdown: The MCP tools and packet schemas name the old blocks. Do item 10 first so there is one contract to update instead of seven.

items.title: One export contract
items.summary: Seven export shapes become two files: the model with decisions merged in, and a decisions document both people and agents can read.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown: `slug.dossier.json` is the model with the reader's state already applied, which is what "merged JSON" is today. `slug.decisions.md` is the pick line, the notes, and the verdicts as Markdown with a small JSON front matter. Source, state packet, handoff, prompt, digest, and Markdown export go away as separate names. Copy for agent copies the decisions document. The MCP server exposes two read tools and one write tool over the same two shapes.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Never has to choose between five kinds of JSON. There is the document and there is what they decided.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Reads one Markdown document to learn what was decided and one JSON file to rebuild. The packet schemas shrink to two.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Items 8 and 9 become tractable, and the CLI's export subcommand loses most of its flags.

facets.label: Risk
facets.markdown: Workspaces and release evidence consume the state and handoff packets today. Give them the decisions document and a compatibility reader for old packets in 0.7.

items.title: One theme
items.summary: Skins, theme packs, and the in-artifact Theme Studio retire in favor of one default look with light and dark, and a single accent override.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown: The skin layer and the theme pack list are removed from the generator. The new default look is the one on this page. `meta.theme.accent` and `meta.fonts` are the only presentation fields. Theme Studio survives only inside serve, as a way to preview an accent and copy the one line into the JSON.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Every Dossier they open looks like the same product, which is what a document format should do.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Stops choosing between berry, forest, console-slate, and studio presets. There is nothing to get wrong.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: Around 20 KB of CSS and the whole of the skins module disappear. The design record shrinks to one page.

facets.label: Risk
facets.markdown: Console Slate was built for dense process pages and this look is airier. Test the implementation-packet and incident examples in the new shell before retiring the skin.

items.title: Skill and starters rewrite
items.summary: The skill teaches kinds and facets instead of a block catalog, and every starter is regenerated in the new format.

facets.label: How it works
facets.markdown: SKILL.md is rewritten around one sentence per kind, the facet vocabulary, and the rule set for items: numbered, sized, with effort and impact, facets in fixed order. The blocks reference shrinks to the consolidated catalog. Starters for the six kinds are regenerated and each one builds to a page shaped like this one. The MCP server gains a tool that lists kinds and their facets, so agents that do not load the skill still author correctly.

facets.label: Reader
facets.markdown: Gets consistent documents from any agent, because the instructions the agent followed are short enough to be followed.

facets.label: Agent
facets.markdown: Loads a skill it can hold entirely in context. The first draft is right more often, which is the whole loop.

facets.label: Unlocks
facets.markdown: The README opens with one prompt and one screenshot instead of a feature map.

items.title: React port parity
items.summary: Keep it, but it follows items 8 and 9 rather than leading them. Its job in 0.7 is to render the reader runtime and nothing more.

items.title: Workspaces and release evidence
items.summary: Untouched in 0.7 beyond consuming the decisions document from item 10. They are not part of the fractured feeling.

items.title: Packs and plugins
items.summary: Keep. Add one rule: a plugin ships markup and CSS, never runtime JavaScript, so packs cannot undo item 8.

items.title: Mermaid and Playwright optionals
items.summary: Keep as install-on-demand. The degrade-to-hint behavior already matches the spirit of the release.

items.title: Hosted Studio with Monaco
items.summary: Still deferred, as the design record says. Item 8 makes it possible later without touching the artifact.
